temperature.title: Air temperature, 2 m
temperature.note: July 2024 monthly air temperature about 2 m above the surface. Yellow and red are warmer; blue and purple are colder.
temperature.citation: Gelaro, R., and others (2017), The Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2), Journal of Climate. Map: NASA GIBS layer MERRA2_2m_Air_Temperature_Monthly, July 2024.

ice-water.title: Ocean, sea ice, and snow
ice-water.source: ETOPO1 plus AMSR2 sea ice (March 2024) and MODIS snow (15 Jan 2024)
ice-water.note: Blue is ocean and brown is land, from ETOPO1. Sea ice is the March 2024 AMSR2 concentration. Snow is the 15 January 2024 MODIS snow cover, including the Antarctic ice sheet.
ice-water.citation: Amante, C., and B. W. Eakins (2009), ETOPO1 1 arc-minute global relief, NOAA. Sea ice: JAXA AMSR2 via NASA GIBS AMSRU2_Sea_Ice_Concentration_25km, March 2024. Snow: NASA MODIS Terra NDSI snow cover, 15 January 2024.

geology.title: Geologic units
geology.source: Geological Survey of Canada world geology, Kirkham, Chorlton, and Carriere 1995
geology.note: Each color is a rock unit on the generalized geologic map of the world, in the same simple-cylindrical frame as the Moon and Mars. Blue is ocean. Pale blue on Antarctica is ice where the source map has no rock unit.
geology.citation: Kirkham, R. V., L. B. Chorlton, and J. J. Carriere, 1995, Generalized geology of the world, Geological Survey of Canada Open File 2915. Map image: USGS Mineral Resources Program WMS, EPSG:4326.

weather.title: Rain and snow rate
weather.note: One day of NASA IMERG precipitation. Green is lighter rain and red is heavier. Dark areas had little or no precipitation that day.
weather.citation: Huffman, G. J., and others, NASA IMERG. Map: NASA GIBS layer IMERG_Precipitation_Rate for 15 July 2024.

light.title: Blue Marble
light.source: NASA Blue Marble Next Generation, August 2004
light.note: Cloud-free view of reflected sunlight. Ice and desert are bright; forest and ocean are darker.
light.citation: Stöckli, R., E. Vermote, N. Saleous, R. Simmon, and D. Herring, The Blue Marble Next Generation, NASA. Map: NASA GIBS BlueMarble_NextGeneration, August 2004.

radiation.title: Outgoing longwave radiation
radiation.note: Heat radiation leaving the top of the atmosphere in July 2018. Deserts and the tropics radiate more; Antarctica radiates less.
radiation.citation: Loeb, N. G., and others, CERES Energy Balanced and Filled top-of-atmosphere fluxes. Map: NASA GIBS CERES_EBAF_TOA_Longwave_Flux_All_Sky_Monthly, July 2018.

temperature.title: Hottest surface temperature
temperature.note: The hottest temperature Diviner recorded in each 0.5° cell, from July 2009 through April 2015. Dark maria get hotter than the bright highlands. The poles are included.
temperature.citation: Williams, J.-P., D. A. Paige, B. T. Greenhagen, and E. Sefton-Nash (2017), The global surface temperatures of the Moon as measured by the Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment, Icarus 283, 300–325.

ice-water.title: Coldest surface temperature
ice-water.note: The coldest temperature in each cell. Water ice is stable where the surface stays below about 110 K, which on this map is the bright polar ground. Most of the Moon is too warm.
ice-water.citation: Williams, J.-P., and others (2017), Icarus 283, 300–325, minimum bolometric temperature. Ice stability near 110 K: Paige, D. A., and others (2010), Science 330, 479–482.

geology.title: Geologic units
geology.source: USGS unified geologic map, Fortezzo, Spudis, and Harrel 2020
geology.note: Each color is a rock unit on the 1:5,000,000 unified map, drawn in the same simple-cylindrical frame as the other Moon maps. Maria, highlands, and crater ejecta are separate colors.
geology.citation: Fortezzo, C. M., P. D. Spudis, and S. L. Harrel (2020), Release of the digital unified global geologic map of the Moon at 1:5,000,000 scale. USGS raster, simple cylindrical, public domain.

weather.title: Day–night temperature swing
weather.note: The Moon has no atmosphere, so it has no wind, clouds, or storms. This is the change from the coldest to the hottest temperature of the ground, which is how the surface environment changes through a lunar day.
weather.citation: Williams, J.-P., and others (2017), Icarus 283, 300–325. The map is the Diviner bolometric maximum minus the minimum on the same 0.5° grid.

light.title: Reflected sunlight
light.note: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Wide Angle Camera mosaic. The dark maria are basaltic lava; the highlands are brighter.
light.citation: USGS Astrogeology WMS, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Wide Angle Camera global mosaic, simple cylindrical.

radiation.title: Heat leaving at midnight
radiation.note: Infrared power the surface radiates at local midnight, from the measured midnight temperature. Rock stays warmer, and radiates more, than dust. This is heat radiation, not a cosmic-ray dose.
radiation.citation: Williams, J.-P., and others (2017), Icarus 283, 300–325, bolometric temperature at local hour 0. Power is σT⁴ with σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/m²/K⁴.

temperature.title: Afternoon surface temperature
temperature.source: MGS TES afternoon temperature, Mars Year 25
temperature.note: Surface temperature retrieved from TES infrared spectra near 14:00 local time, averaged in 5° cells across Mars Year 25. Empty cells, mostly near the winter pole of a given season, are dark.
temperature.citation: Smith, M. D. (2004), Interannual variability in TES atmospheric observations of Mars, Icarus 167, 148–165. Values from the NASA PDS TES column-opacity bundle (Montabone, Smith, Wolff, and Cantor) for all of Mars Year 25.

ice-water.title: Hydrogen and water ice
ice-water.source: Mars Odyssey neutron spectrometer, epithermal neutrons
ice-water.note: Fewer epithermal neutrons means more hydrogen in the top metre of soil. In these first 25.7 days of mapping the southern high latitudes are the strong hydrogen signal. The unmeasured polar rows are dark.
ice-water.citation: Feldman, W. C., and others (2002), Global distribution of neutrons from Mars: results from Mars Odyssey, Science 297, 75–78. NASA PDS table ns_epithermal_020917.

geology.title: Geologic units
geology.source: USGS geologic map of Mars, Tanaka and others 2014
geology.note: Each color is a rock unit from the 1:20,000,000 geologic map, drawn in the same simple-cylindrical frame as the Moon. Brown is the old southern highlands, green is the northern plains, and red and yellow are volcanic rock.
geology.citation: Tanaka, K. L., J. A. Skinner, J. M. Dohm, R. P. Irwin, E. J. Kolb, C. M. Fortezzo, T. Platz, G. G. Michael, and T. M. Hare (2014), Geologic map of Mars, USGS Scientific Investigations Map 3292. Rasterized from the published degree-coordinate shapefile.

weather.title: Dust in the atmosphere
weather.source: MGS TES column dust optical depth, Mars Year 25
weather.note: Dust opacity at 9.3 μm, averaged in 5° cells across Mars Year 25. Southern summer raises the dust. Empty cells are dark.
weather.citation: Montabone, L., and others (2015), Eight-year climatology of dust optical depth on Mars, Icarus 251, 65–95. Retrievals: NASA PDS TES infrared column dust optical depth for all of Mars Year 25.

light.title: Viking color mosaic
light.note: Viking orbiter color mosaic. The bright spots at the poles are ice. Hellas is the bright basin in the south.
light.citation: USGS Astrogeology WMS, Viking Mars Digital Image Model 2.1 color mosaic, simple cylindrical.

radiation.title: Fast neutrons from cosmic rays
radiation.source: Mars Odyssey neutron spectrometer, fast neutrons
radiation.note: Fast neutrons made when cosmic rays hit the surface. High ground such as Olympus Mons has a thinner atmosphere overhead, so more fast neutrons escape. This is a measured neutron flux, not a dose in milligray.
radiation.citation: Feldman, W. C., and others (2002), Science 297, 75–78. NASA PDS table ns_fast_020917, the first 25.7 days of mapping.
